extraction.name: Prompted Textures Dataset (PTD)
extraction.description: A synthetic texture dataset containing 246,285 images across 56 texture classes, generated from descriptive prompts using Stable Diffusion and curated through frequency, patch variance, and CLIP-score filtering. The final dataset is balanced across texture classes and designed to support texture-based research.
extraction.creator: Blaine Hoak and Patrick McDaniel
extraction.citeAs: Blaine Hoak and Patrick McDaniel. On Synthetic Texture Datasets: Challenges, Creation, and Curation. arXiv:2409.10297v3 [cs.CV], 9 May 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors constructed 96,768 unique texture prompts by combining artistic, spatial, color-enhancer, color, and texture descriptors. They began with 47 texture classes from the Describable Textures Dataset and added nine meaningfully different classes sourced from additional texture lists. Prompts were supplied to Stable Diffusion from HuggingFace. Five images not flagged by the model's safety filter were generated per prompt, yielding 483,840 images before refinement. Three subsequent filtering stages produced 246,285 final images.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw images were synthesized using Stable Diffusion from constructed text prompts, rather than collected as photographs. Texture descriptors originated from the 47 classes of the Describable Textures Dataset and additional texture lists, including '400 Words to Describe Texture.' Additional descriptor categories were inspired by the seven basic elements of art.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Prompts combined one descriptor from each category in standard English adjective order: artistic, spatial, color enhancer, color, and texture. For safety-filter analysis, the generation pipeline was temporarily modified to disable filtering so flagged images could be recorded with their original content. Flagged images were excluded from the released dataset, and generation was repeated to obtain five unflagged images per prompt.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images flagged as NSFW were excluded. Refinement then applied three class-balanced filtering stages. First, Fourier transforms and power spectra were used to calculate the frequency radius splitting cumulative energy evenly; only the top 80% of images with the highest frequency cutoffs were retained within each texture class to remove object-like images. Second, images were divided into non-overlapping 50-by-50-pixel patches, and the variance of patch mean intensities was calculated; the bottom 20% within each class were removed to eliminate homogeneous images. Third, the bottom 20% of images by CLIP cosine similarity between image and prompt embeddings were removed within each class to improve prompt alignment.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Images were generated from prompts specifying one of 56 texture classes and additional descriptive attributes. For human quality evaluation, nine participants each evaluated 100 randomly ordered images sampled before refinement, with no duplicate images within or between participant sets. Each participant rated overall image quality and how well the image represented its provided descriptor on separate scales from 1 to 5, where 1 was worst and 5 was best. Participants could also provide comments about observed trends. This evaluation covered 900 unique images, rather than the entire dataset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human quality and representativeness ratings were averaged across images remaining at each cumulative refinement stage. Mean quality increased from 3.87 before refinement to 4.00 after all stages, and mean representativeness increased from 3.56 to 3.72. The authors report overall improvements of 3.4% and 4.5%, respectively. Human representativeness scores and optional comments were also compared with CLIP scores to analyze descriptor combinations and prompt-image alignment.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For the 900 images in the human evaluation, one participant provided two ratings per image: overall quality and descriptor representativeness.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: CLIP was used for automated prompt-image alignment scoring and filtering. Stable Diffusion's content safety filter used CLIP scores against NSFW content words to flag generated images.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance model interpretability, bias analysis, robustness, and trustworthiness by enabling research into learned texture-object associations and texture bias. Although the authors found no explicit content in safety-flagged images, they excluded those images from the public release for ethical reasons. They highlight the need for safety filters that better handle abstract or texture-based content.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Safety filtering disproportionately flagged certain texture descriptors: up to 60% of initial generated images were flagged, and nearly all prompts containing 'paisley' produced at least one flagged image among five generated images. Flagged images generally appeared smoother and more muted despite showing no clear explicit content. Fourier analysis comparing mean power spectra with the Describable Textures Dataset indicated that the final dataset was not biased toward a particular frequency.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Stable Diffusion is not explicitly designed to generate textures and can produce object-like or overly homogeneous images. Quality varies across texture classes, with structured textures such as grid and polka-dotted achieving worse evaluation scores than textures such as hairy and flaky. Some descriptor combinations, particularly subtle textures paired with 'muted' or 'earthy,' yield lower prompt-alignment scores. Human evaluators reported that requested symmetry was sometimes absent and that color descriptors could alter backgrounds. Inception and FID metrics were originally designed for object-based datasets, although the authors use them to assess textures against a real-world baseline.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Texture-based research, analysis of high-level features learned by models, discovery of texture-object associations, measurement of texture bias, and research into interpretability, robustness, and security vulnerabilities. The dataset has been used to develop Texture Object Association Values, which analyze model responses to texture images to quantify associations between textures and object classes. The paper demonstrates this use on ResNet50.
